specStatements.text: Students should be able to describe the principles of hormonal coordination and control by the human endocrine system.

The endocrine system is composed of glands which secrete chemicals called hormones directly into the bloodstream. The blood carries the hormone to a target organ where it produces an effect. Compared to the nervous system the effects are slower but act for longer.

The pituitary gland in the brain is a 'master gland' which secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions. These hormones in turn act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released to bring about effects.
Students should be able to identify the position of the following on a diagram of the human body: pituitary gland; pancreas; thyroid; adrenal gland; ovary; testes.
Blood glucose concentration is monitored and controlled by the pancreas.

If the blood glucose concentration is too high, the pancreas produces the hormone insulin that causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells. In liver and muscle cells excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.
Students should be able to explain how insulin controls blood glucose (sugar) levels in the body.
Type 1 diabetes is a disorder in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin. It is characterised by uncontrolled high blood glucose levels and is normally treated with insulin injections.

In Type 2 diabetes the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas. A carbohydrate controlled diet and an exercise regime are common treatments. Obesity is a risk factor for Type 2 diabetes.
Students should be able to compare Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes and explain how they can be treated.
Students should be able to extract information and interpret data from graphs that show the effect of insulin in blood glucose levels in both people with diabetes and people without diabetes.
If the blood glucose concentration is too low, the pancreas produces the hormone glucagon that causes glycogen to be converted into glucose and released into the blood.
Students should be able to explain how glucagon interacts with insulin in a negative feedback cycle to control blood glucose (sugar) levels in the body.
Students should be able to explain the effect on cells of osmotic changes in body fluids.
Water leaves the body via the lungs during exhalation.
Water, ions and urea are lost from the skin in sweat.
There is no control over water, ion or urea loss by the lungs or skin.
Excess water, ions and urea are removed via the kidneys in the urine.
If body cells lose or gain too much water by osmosis they do not function efficiently.

The digestion of proteins from the diet results in excess amino acids which need to be excreted safely. In the liver these amino acids are deaminated to form ammonia. Ammonia is toxic and so it is immediately converted to urea for safe excretion.
Students should be able to describe the function of kidneys in maintaining the water balance of the body.
The kidneys produce urine by filtration of the blood and selective reabsorption of useful substances such as glucose, some ions and water.
Knowledge of other parts of the urinary system, the structure of the kidney and the structure of a nephron is not required.
Students should be able to translate tables and bar charts of glucose, ions and urea before and after filtration.
Students should be able to describe the effect of ADH on the permeability of the kidney tubules.

The water level in the body is controlled by the hormone ADH which acts on the kidney tubules. ADH is released by the pituitary gland when the blood is too concentrated and it causes more water to be reabsorbed back into the blood from the kidney tubules. This is controlled by negative feedback.
People who suffer from kidney failure may be treated by organ transplant or by using kidney dialysis. Students should know the basic principles of dialysis.
Students should be able to describe the roles of hormones in human reproduction, including the menstrual cycle.
During puberty reproductive hormones cause secondary sex characteristics to develop.
Oestrogen is the main female reproductive hormone produced in the ovary. At puberty eggs begin to mature and one is released approximately every 28 days. This is called ovulation.
Testosterone is the main male reproductive hormone produced by the testes and it stimulates sperm production.

Several hormones are involved in the menstrual cycle of a woman. Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) causes maturation of an egg in the ovary.; Luteinising hormone (LH) stimulates the release of the egg.; Oestrogen and progesterone are involved in maintaining the uterus lining.
Students should be able to explain the interactions of FSH, oestrogen, LH and progesterone, in the control of the menstrual cycle.
Students should be able to extract and interpret data from graphs showing hormone levels during the menstrual cycle.
Students should be able to evaluate the different hormonal and non-hormonal methods of contraception.
Fertility can be controlled by a variety of hormonal and non-hormonal methods of contraception.

These include: oral contraceptives that contain hormones to inhibit FSH production so that no eggs mature; injection, implant or skin patch of slow release progesterone to inhibit the maturation and release of eggs for a number of months or years; barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms which prevent the sperm reaching an egg; intrauterine devices which prevent the implantation of an embryo or release a hormone; spermicidal agents which kill or disable sperm; abstaining from intercourse when an egg may be in the oviduct; surgical methods of male and female sterilisation.
Students should be able to explain the use of hormones in modern reproductive technologies to treat infertility.
This includes giving FSH and LH in a 'fertility drug' to a woman. She may then become pregnant in the normal way.

In Vitro Fertilisation (IVF) treatment. IVF involves giving a mother FSH and LH to stimulate the maturation of several eggs.; The eggs are collected from the mother and fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory.; The fertilised eggs develop into embryos.; At the stage when they are tiny balls of cells, one or two embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus (womb).

Although fertility treatment gives a woman the chance to have a baby of her own: it is very emotionally and physically stressful; the success rates are not high; it can lead to multiple births which are a risk to both the babies and the mother.
Students should be able to explain the roles of thyroxine and adrenaline in the body.

Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress. It increases the heart rate and boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles, preparing the body for 'flight or fight'.
Thyroxine from the thyroid gland stimulates the basal metabolic rate. It plays an important role in growth and development.
Thyroxine levels are controlled by negative feedback.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of other parts of the urinary system, the structure of the kidney and the structure of a nephron is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Knowledge of other parts of the urinary system, the structure of the kidney and the structure of a nephron is not required, so no concept, misconception or question in this set refers to the ureter, bladder, urethra, cortex, medulla, nephron, glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, loop of Henle or collecting duct. Kidney content is limited to what the specification states: filtration of the blood, selective reabsorption of useful substances such as glucose, some ions and water, the removal of excess water, ions and urea in the urine, and the effect of ADH on 'the kidney tubules', which is the only structural term the specification itself uses.

concepts.definition: The system composed of glands which secrete chemicals called hormones directly into the bloodstream.
A chemical secreted by a gland directly into the bloodstream; the blood carries the hormone to a target organ where it produces an effect.
Compared to the nervous system, the effects brought about by the endocrine system are slower but act for longer.

A 'master gland' in the brain which secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions; these hormones in turn act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released to bring about effects.

On a diagram of the human body: the pituitary gland is in the brain; the thyroid is in the neck; the adrenal glands are on top of the kidneys; the pancreas lies behind the stomach; the ovaries are in the lower abdomen; the testes are below the abdomen in the scrotum.
The gland that monitors and controls blood glucose concentration by producing hormones.
The hormone produced by the pancreas if the blood glucose concentration is too high; it causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells.
The storage substance made in liver and muscle cells, where excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.
A disorder in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, characterised by uncontrolled high blood glucose levels and normally treated with insulin injections.
A disorder in which the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas; a carbohydrate controlled diet and an exercise regime are common treatments, and obesity is a risk factor.
The hormone produced by the pancreas if the blood glucose concentration is too low; it causes glycogen to be converted into glucose and released into the blood.

Control in which a level that has moved away from normal brings about a response that returns it to normal; it controls blood glucose through insulin and glucagon, the water level through ADH, and thyroxine levels.
If body cells lose or gain too much water by osmosis they do not function efficiently.
Water leaves the body via the lungs during exhalation, and there is no control over this loss.
The liquid lost from the skin, containing water, ions and urea; there is no control over water, ion or urea loss by the skin.
A waste substance lost from the skin in sweat and removed, with excess water and ions, via the kidneys in the urine.

The process in the liver in which excess amino acids from the digestion of dietary protein are deaminated to form ammonia; ammonia is toxic and so it is immediately converted to urea for safe excretion.
The first stage by which the kidneys produce urine, in which the blood is filtered.
The taking back into the blood of useful substances such as glucose, some ions and water after the blood has been filtered by the kidneys.

The hormone that controls the water level in the body; it is released by the pituitary gland when the blood is too concentrated and acts on the kidney tubules, making them more permeable so that more water is reabsorbed back into the blood.

People who suffer from kidney failure may be treated by organ transplant or by using kidney dialysis; in dialysis the blood flows next to a dialysis fluid that contains no urea but the same concentration of useful substances as normal blood, so urea passes out of the blood while glucose and useful ions are not lost.
The features that develop during puberty, caused by reproductive hormones.
The main female reproductive hormone, produced in the ovary; with progesterone it is involved in maintaining the uterus lining.
The release of an egg from the ovary; from puberty eggs begin to mature and one is released approximately every 28 days.
The main male reproductive hormone, produced by the testes; it stimulates sperm production.
A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which causes maturation of an egg in the ovary.
A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which stimulates the release of the egg.
A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which, with oestrogen, is involved in maintaining the uterus lining.

Methods of controlling fertility that use hormones: oral contraceptives that contain hormones to inhibit FSH production so that no eggs mature; and injection, implant or skin patch of slow release progesterone to inhibit the maturation and release of eggs for a number of months or years. Some intrauterine devices also release a hormone.

Methods of controlling fertility that do not use hormones: barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms which prevent the sperm reaching an egg; intrauterine devices which prevent the implantation of an embryo; spermicidal agents which kill or disable sperm; abstaining from intercourse when an egg may be in the oviduct; and surgical methods of male and female sterilisation.
A drug containing FSH and LH given to a woman to treat infertility, after which she may become pregnant in the normal way.

Fertility treatment in which a mother is given FSH and LH to stimulate the maturation of several eggs; the eggs are collected from the mother and fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory, the fertilised eggs develop into embryos, and at the stage when they are tiny balls of cells one or two embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus. It is very emotionally and physically stressful, the success rates are not high, and it can lead to multiple births which are a risk to both the babies and the mother.

A hormone produced by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress; it increases the heart rate and boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles, preparing the body for 'flight or fight'.
A hormone from the thyroid gland which stimulates the basal metabolic rate and plays an important role in growth and development; its level is controlled by negative feedback.

misconceptions.question: How does a hormone get from the gland that makes it to the organ where it has its effect?
misconceptions.correct: The gland secretes the hormone directly into the bloodstream, and the blood carries it to a target organ.
misconceptions.misconception: Hormones are carried along nerves, in the same way that nerve impulses travel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hormonal and nervous coordination are taught together, and both are described as ways of sending information around the body, so students merge the two and give hormones the pathway that belongs to nerve impulses.
misconceptions.correction: The endocrine system is composed of glands which secrete chemicals called hormones directly into the bloodstream; the blood carries the hormone to a target organ where it produces an effect.

misconceptions.question: A hormone is carried in the blood to every part of the body. Does it produce an effect everywhere?
misconceptions.correct: No. Although the blood carries it everywhere, the hormone produces its effect at a target organ.
misconceptions.misconception: A hormone produces an effect in every organ that the blood carries it to.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that the blood reaches all organs, and then assume that anything carried in the blood must act on all of them, overlooking the idea of a target organ.
misconceptions.correction: The blood carries the hormone to a target organ where it produces an effect.

misconceptions.question: How do the effects of the endocrine system compare with those of the nervous system?
misconceptions.correct: Compared to the nervous system the effects are slower but act for longer.
misconceptions.misconception: Hormones act faster than nerve impulses and their effects wear off more quickly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Adrenaline is often the first hormone students meet and it appears to act instantly in a frightening situation, so they generalise from it and reverse the comparison the specification makes.
misconceptions.correction: Compared to the nervous system the effects of the endocrine system are slower but act for longer.

misconceptions.question: What does the pituitary gland do when it secretes a hormone?
misconceptions.correct: Its hormones act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released to bring about effects.
misconceptions.misconception: The pituitary gland brings about all of its effects directly, without any other gland being involved.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The label 'master gland' suggests a gland that does everything itself, so students picture the pituitary acting straight on the body rather than acting through the glands it controls.
misconceptions.correction: The pituitary gland secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions, and these hormones in turn act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released to bring about effects.

misconceptions.question: Where are the pituitary gland, thyroid, adrenal glands and pancreas found in the body?
misconceptions.correct: The pituitary gland is in the brain, the thyroid is in the neck, the adrenal glands are on top of the kidneys and the pancreas lies behind the stomach.
misconceptions.misconception: The names of the endocrine glands can be attached to any of the positions shown, so the pituitary gland can be placed below the stomach and the adrenal gland inside the brain.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The glands are learned as a list of names and functions rather than as positions on a diagram, so when a diagram is labelled students guess and swap glands that they have never located.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to identify the position of the pituitary gland, pancreas, thyroid, adrenal gland, ovary and testes on a diagram of the human body.

misconceptions.question: When does the pancreas produce insulin?
misconceptions.correct: The pancreas produces insulin if the blood glucose concentration is too high.
misconceptions.misconception: Insulin is produced when the blood glucose concentration is too low, in order to raise it again.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate insulin with diabetes and with feeling faint from low blood sugar, and injections are given to make a person better, so they attach insulin to the low glucose situation instead of the high one.
misconceptions.correction: If the blood glucose concentration is too high, the pancreas produces the hormone insulin that causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells.

misconceptions.question: Where does insulin cause glucose to be converted into glycogen?
misconceptions.correct: Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells, and in liver and muscle cells excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.
misconceptions.misconception: Insulin converts the glucose into glycogen while it is still in the blood.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember the pair of words 'glucose to glycogen' but not the step before it, so they leave the glucose in the blood where the hormone met it instead of moving it into cells first.
misconceptions.correction: Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells; in liver and muscle cells excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.

misconceptions.question: What does glucagon do?
misconceptions.correct: Glucagon causes glycogen to be converted into glucose and released into the blood.
misconceptions.misconception: Glucagon is just another name for glycogen, and like insulin it lowers the blood glucose concentration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words glucagon, glycogen and glucose look and sound almost the same, so students treat them as one idea and give glucagon the job of the hormone they met first.
misconceptions.correction: If the blood glucose concentration is too low, the pancreas produces the hormone glucagon that causes glycogen to be converted into glucose and released into the blood.

misconceptions.question: What has gone wrong in the body of a person with Type 2 diabetes?
misconceptions.correct: The body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas.
misconceptions.misconception: In Type 2 diabetes the pancreas has stopped producing insulin.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both types of diabetes are described as uncontrolled blood glucose, so students give them the same cause and apply the failure of the pancreas, which they met first in Type 1, to both.
misconceptions.correction: In Type 2 diabetes the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas; it is Type 1 diabetes in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin.

misconceptions.question: How is Type 1 diabetes normally treated?
misconceptions.correct: It is normally treated with insulin injections.
misconceptions.misconception: Type 1 diabetes is caused by eating too much sugar and is treated with a controlled diet and exercise.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diet and exercise are heavily publicised as the answer to diabetes, and the two types are rarely separated in everyday reporting, so the treatment for Type 2 is applied to Type 1 as well.
misconceptions.correction: Type 1 diabetes is a disorder in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin and is normally treated with insulin injections; a carbohydrate controlled diet and an exercise regime are common treatments for Type 2 diabetes.

misconceptions.question: Is the loss of water from the lungs and the skin controlled by the body?
misconceptions.correct: No. There is no control over water, ion or urea loss by the lungs or skin.
misconceptions.misconception: The body controls how much water it loses in sweat and in exhaled breath, in the same way that it controls water loss in urine.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sweating is a controlled response in temperature regulation, so students assume the water lost in sweat is also being regulated, and they extend the idea of control to breathing as well.
misconceptions.correction: Water leaves the body via the lungs during exhalation, and water, ions and urea are lost from the skin in sweat; there is no control over water, ion or urea loss by the lungs or skin.

misconceptions.question: What is lost from the skin in sweat?
misconceptions.correct: Water, ions and urea are lost from the skin in sweat.
misconceptions.misconception: Sweat is only water, so nothing else is lost from the skin.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sweat is met first as a cooling mechanism that works by the evaporation of water, so students record only the water and do not connect sweat with the loss of ions and urea.
misconceptions.correction: Water, ions and urea are lost from the skin in sweat.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter if body cells gain or lose water by osmosis?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. If body cells lose or gain too much water by osmosis they do not function efficiently.
misconceptions.misconception: Cells carry on working normally however much water they gain or lose, because the extra water is simply stored or replaced.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Osmosis is first met in plant tissue investigations, where gaining water makes a cell firm and seems to do it good, so students do not connect osmotic change with cells working less efficiently.
misconceptions.correction: If body cells lose or gain too much water by osmosis they do not function efficiently, which is why the water level in the body is controlled.

misconceptions.question: Body fluids become too dilute. Which way does water move across the cell membranes?
misconceptions.correct: Water moves into the cells by osmosis, so the cells gain water.
misconceptions.misconception: When the body fluids become too dilute the cells lose water by osmosis.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that osmosis is about water moving but not the direction rule, so they pair 'too much water outside' with 'water leaves the cell' without comparing the concentrations either side of the membrane.
misconceptions.correction: Water moves by osmosis into cells when the body fluids around them become too dilute, and if body cells gain too much water they do not function efficiently.

misconceptions.question: Where is urea made in the body?
misconceptions.correct: Urea is made in the liver, from the ammonia formed when excess amino acids are deaminated.
misconceptions.misconception: Urea is made in the kidneys, because that is where it is found in the urine.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The kidney is the organ students associate with urea because urine is made there, and the liver is met in a different topic, so the place where urea is removed is taken to be the place where it is made.
misconceptions.correction: In the liver excess amino acids are deaminated to form ammonia; ammonia is toxic and so it is immediately converted to urea for safe excretion, and the urea is then removed via the kidneys in the urine.

misconceptions.question: Are useful substances such as glucose filtered out of the blood by the kidneys?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The kidneys produce urine by filtration of the blood and then selective reabsorption of useful substances such as glucose, some ions and water.
misconceptions.misconception: The kidneys filter out only the waste substances, so useful substances never leave the blood.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Filtration is pictured as a sieve that separates good from bad in one step, which removes any need for a second stage, so selective reabsorption is left out of the explanation.
misconceptions.correction: The kidneys produce urine by filtration of the blood and selective reabsorption of useful substances such as glucose, some ions and water.

misconceptions.question: When is ADH released, and what does it do?
misconceptions.correct: ADH is released by the pituitary gland when the blood is too concentrated, and it causes more water to be reabsorbed back into the blood from the kidney tubules.
misconceptions.misconception: ADH is released when the blood is too dilute, and it makes the body produce more urine to get rid of the extra water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link a hormone with the action of removing a problem substance, so they pair ADH with getting rid of water rather than with saving it, and they reverse the condition that triggers its release.
misconceptions.correction: ADH is released by the pituitary gland when the blood is too concentrated; it acts on the kidney tubules, making them more permeable so that more water is reabsorbed back into the blood. This is controlled by negative feedback.

misconceptions.question: In kidney dialysis, which substances pass out of the blood into the dialysis fluid?
misconceptions.correct: Urea passes out of the blood into the dialysis fluid, while glucose and useful ions are not lost.
misconceptions.misconception: Dialysis cleans the blood by removing everything dissolved in it, so glucose and useful ions are taken out along with the urea.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Dialysis is described as cleaning or washing the blood, which suggests that everything dissolved is stripped out, and students do not think about what the dialysis fluid itself contains.
misconceptions.correction: The dialysis fluid contains no urea, but it contains the same concentration of useful substances as normal blood, so urea passes out of the blood while glucose and useful ions are not lost.

misconceptions.question: Which hormone matures an egg and which hormone releases it?
misconceptions.correct: Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) causes maturation of an egg in the ovary and luteinising hormone (LH) stimulates the release of the egg.
misconceptions.misconception: FSH releases the egg and LH makes the egg mature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both hormones come from the same gland, act on the same organ and are learned as a pair of initials, so the two jobs are easily swapped when the names are not linked to their meanings.
misconceptions.correction: Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) causes maturation of an egg in the ovary; luteinising hormone (LH) stimulates the release of the egg.

misconceptions.question: Which glands produce oestrogen and testosterone?
misconceptions.correct: Oestrogen is produced in the ovary and testosterone is produced by the testes.
misconceptions.misconception: The pituitary gland is the master gland, so it produces the reproductive hormones oestrogen and testosterone as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that the pituitary controls reproduction and that it is the master gland, and they take control of a process to mean production of every hormone involved in it.
misconceptions.correction: Oestrogen is the main female reproductive hormone produced in the ovary; testosterone is the main male reproductive hormone produced by the testes.

misconceptions.question: Which hormones are involved in maintaining the uterus lining?
misconceptions.correct: Oestrogen and progesterone are involved in maintaining the uterus lining.
misconceptions.misconception: FSH and LH maintain the uterus lining, while oestrogen and progesterone control the egg.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Four hormones are learned at once in one cycle, and students separate them into the pair with initials and the pair with names rather than by what each one does, so the two roles are exchanged.
misconceptions.correction: FSH causes maturation of an egg in the ovary and LH stimulates the release of the egg; oestrogen and progesterone are involved in maintaining the uterus lining.

misconceptions.question: How do oral contraceptives prevent pregnancy?
misconceptions.correct: They contain hormones to inhibit FSH production so that no eggs mature.
misconceptions.misconception: The contraceptive pill works by killing or disabling the sperm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All contraceptives are met as one list with one purpose, so students give them one shared mechanism, and stopping the sperm is the most obvious way to prevent fertilisation.
misconceptions.correction: Oral contraceptives contain hormones to inhibit FSH production so that no eggs mature; it is spermicidal agents that kill or disable sperm.

misconceptions.question: Do barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms use hormones?
misconceptions.correct: No. Barrier methods prevent the sperm reaching an egg and do not contain hormones.
misconceptions.misconception: Condoms and diaphragms work by releasing hormones that stop eggs maturing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The methods are listed together under contraception and the hormonal ones are studied in most detail, so students carry the hormone explanation across to the methods that are purely physical.
misconceptions.correction: Barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms prevent the sperm reaching an egg; only the hormonal methods, such as oral contraceptives and slow release progesterone, work by altering hormone levels.

misconceptions.question: What does an intrauterine device do, and what does a spermicidal agent do?
misconceptions.correct: Intrauterine devices prevent the implantation of an embryo or release a hormone, and spermicidal agents kill or disable sperm.
misconceptions.misconception: Intrauterine devices work by killing sperm and spermicidal agents work by preventing an embryo implanting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are non-hormonal methods learned in the same list, and neither is linked to a familiar picture of how it works, so the two mechanisms are attached to the wrong method.
misconceptions.correction: Intrauterine devices prevent the implantation of an embryo or release a hormone; spermicidal agents kill or disable sperm.

misconceptions.question: Where are the eggs fertilised in IVF treatment?
misconceptions.correct: The eggs are collected from the mother and fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory.
misconceptions.misconception: In IVF the hormones are given so that fertilisation happens inside the mother's body in the usual way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fertility treatment is met as one idea, and because a fertility drug does lead to a pregnancy in the normal way, students assume IVF works the same way and miss the step outside the body that the name refers to.
misconceptions.correction: IVF involves giving a mother FSH and LH to stimulate the maturation of several eggs; the eggs are collected from the mother and fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory, and at the stage when the fertilised eggs are tiny balls of cells one or two embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus.

misconceptions.question: How successful and how safe is IVF treatment?
misconceptions.correct: The success rates are not high, the treatment is very emotionally and physically stressful, and it can lead to multiple births which are a risk to both the babies and the mother.
misconceptions.misconception: IVF nearly always works and carries no real risk to the mother or the babies.
misconceptions.whyItArises: IVF is reported through the successful births that make the news, and multiple births are presented as happy outcomes, so the failure rate and the risks are rarely part of the story students hear.
misconceptions.correction: Although fertility treatment gives a woman the chance to have a baby of her own, it is very emotionally and physically stressful, the success rates are not high, and it can lead to multiple births which are a risk to both the babies and the mother.

misconceptions.question: Which gland produces adrenaline, and what effect does it have?
misconceptions.correct: Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress, and it increases the heart rate.
misconceptions.misconception: Adrenaline is released by the pituitary gland, because the pituitary controls the response to danger.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The pituitary is remembered as the gland that responds to body conditions and controls other glands, so students make it the source of the hormone released in an emergency instead of naming the gland it is called after.
misconceptions.correction: Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress; it increases the heart rate and boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles, preparing the body for 'flight or fight'.

misconceptions.question: What effect does thyroxine have on the basal metabolic rate?
misconceptions.correct: Thyroxine stimulates the basal metabolic rate.
misconceptions.misconception: Thyroxine lowers the basal metabolic rate, slowing the body's reactions down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Thyroxine is introduced through negative feedback, where the language is all about reducing and inhibiting, so students attach the idea of lowering to the hormone itself rather than to the control of its level.
misconceptions.correction: Thyroxine from the thyroid gland stimulates the basal metabolic rate and plays an important role in growth and development; it is the release of thyroxine that is reduced when its level in the blood is too high.

misconceptions.question: The level of thyroxine in the blood rises above normal. What does negative feedback do?
misconceptions.correct: The release of thyroxine is inhibited, so the level falls back towards normal.
misconceptions.misconception: When a hormone level rises above normal, negative feedback makes the body release even more of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read feedback as the body responding to a rise by doing more of the same, and the word negative is taken to describe the hormone or the situation rather than the reversing of the change.
misconceptions.correction: Thyroxine levels are controlled by negative feedback: a level above normal inhibits the release of thyroxine so that the level returns to normal, in the same way that insulin and glucagon return blood glucose concentration to normal.

mcqs.stem: A gland of the endocrine system secretes a hormone. How does that hormone reach the organ where it produces an effect, and how do its effects compare with those of the nervous system?

options.text: carried along nerves; effects are slower but last longer
options.rationale: A student who believes hormones travel by the same route as nerve impulses picks this. It is wrong because glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream, and the blood carries them to a target organ.

options.text: carried in the blood; effects are faster but end much sooner
options.rationale: A student who generalises from adrenaline appearing to act instantly picks this. It is wrong because compared to the nervous system the effects of hormones are slower but act for longer.

options.text: carried along nerves; effects are faster but end sooner
options.rationale: A student who gives hormones the nervous pathway, and with it the speed of nerve impulses, picks this. It is wrong because hormones are carried in the blood and their effects are slower but act for longer.

options.text: carried in the blood; effects are slower but last longer
options.rationale: Glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream and the blood carries the hormone to a target organ; compared to the nervous system the effects are slower but act for longer.

mcqs.stem: A student labels endocrine glands on a diagram of the human body. Which label has been placed in the correct position?

options.text: the adrenal gland labelled inside the brain
options.rationale: A student who has learned the gland names but not their positions picks this. It is wrong because the adrenal glands are on top of the kidneys; the gland in the brain is the pituitary gland.

options.text: the thyroid gland labelled in the lower neck
options.rationale: The thyroid is found in the neck, and students should be able to identify its position on a diagram of the human body.

options.text: the pituitary gland labelled below the stomach
options.rationale: A student who attaches gland names to any position picks this. It is wrong because the pituitary gland is in the brain; the gland lying behind and below the stomach is the pancreas.

options.text: the pancreas labelled at the base of the brain
options.rationale: A student who has not located the glands on a diagram picks this. It is wrong because the pancreas lies behind the stomach; the gland at the base of the brain is the pituitary gland.

mcqs.stem: Why is the pituitary gland described as a 'master gland'?

options.text: its hormones make other glands release hormones
options.rationale: The pituitary gland secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions, and these act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released.

options.text: its hormones produce all the body effects directly
options.rationale: A student who reads 'master gland' as a gland that does everything itself picks this. It is wrong because the effects are brought about by the other glands that pituitary hormones act on.

options.text: its hormones travel to the glands along nerves
options.rationale: A student who confuses hormonal and nervous coordination picks this. It is wrong because the pituitary secretes its hormones into the blood, which carries them to the other glands.

options.text: its hormones act on every organ in the body
options.rationale: A student who thinks a hormone acts everywhere the blood reaches picks this. It is wrong because pituitary hormones act on other glands as their target organs.

mcqs.stem: After a meal, the blood glucose concentration of a person who does not have diabetes rises above the normal level. What happens next?

options.text: insulin is released and glycogen forms in the blood
options.rationale: A student who believes insulin converts glucose to glycogen in the blood picks this. It is wrong because insulin first causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells.

options.text: insulin is released and so glucose leaves the cells
options.rationale: A student who thinks insulin acts when glucose is too low picks this. It is wrong because insulin is produced when the concentration is too high and moves glucose from the blood into cells.

options.text: insulin is released but the cells fail to respond
options.rationale: A student who applies the Type 2 diabetes situation to everyone picks this. It is wrong because in a person without diabetes the cells do respond, so glucose moves from the blood into them.

options.text: insulin is released and glucose enters the cells
options.rationale: If the blood glucose concentration is too high, the pancreas produces the hormone insulin that causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells.

mcqs.stem: A person's blood glucose concentration is too high. What happens to the excess glucose?

options.text: it is changed into glycogen in the blood
options.rationale: A student who leaves the glucose in the blood when it is converted picks this. It is wrong because glucose is converted to glycogen inside liver and muscle cells, not in the blood.

options.text: it is released from the cells into the blood
options.rationale: A student who thinks insulin is produced when glucose is too low picks this. It is wrong because glucose is released into the blood when the concentration is too low, not too high.

options.text: it is changed into glycogen in the pancreas
options.rationale: A student who places the conversion in the gland that makes the hormone picks this. It is wrong because excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage in liver and muscle cells.

options.text: it moves into cells and is stored as glycogen
options.rationale: Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells, and in liver and muscle cells excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.

mcqs.stem: What causes Type 1 diabetes?

options.text: the body cells no longer respond to insulin
options.rationale: A student who gives both types of diabetes the same cause picks this. It is wrong because cells failing to respond to insulin is Type 2 diabetes, not Type 1.

options.text: the pancreas releases insulin when glucose is low
options.rationale: A student who reverses the trigger for insulin release picks this. It is wrong because insulin is produced when the blood glucose concentration is too high, and Type 1 diabetes is a failure to produce enough of it.

options.text: the pancreas fails to produce enough insulin
options.rationale: Type 1 diabetes is a disorder in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, and it is characterised by uncontrolled high blood glucose levels.

options.text: the pancreas is affected by a person's diet
options.rationale: A student who believes Type 1 diabetes is caused by diet picks this. It is wrong because Type 1 diabetes is a failure of the pancreas to produce sufficient insulin; obesity is a risk factor for Type 2 diabetes.

mcqs.stem: A person with Type 2 diabetes has a normal concentration of insulin in the blood but a high blood glucose concentration. Why?

options.text: their pancreas has completely stopped making insulin
options.rationale: A student who gives Type 2 diabetes the cause of Type 1 picks this. It is wrong because the data show a normal insulin concentration, so the pancreas is still producing insulin.

options.text: their insulin cannot act on glucose in the blood
options.rationale: A student who believes insulin works on glucose while it is in the blood picks this. It is wrong because insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells, and in Type 2 diabetes it is the cells that fail to respond.

options.text: their body cells no longer respond to insulin
options.rationale: In Type 2 diabetes the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas, so glucose is not moved from the blood into the cells even though insulin is present.

options.text: their insulin is released when blood glucose is low
options.rationale: A student who reverses the trigger for insulin release picks this. It is wrong because insulin is produced when the blood glucose concentration is too high.

mcqs.stem: A graph shows blood glucose concentration for two hours after a glucose drink. For a person without diabetes the concentration rises to a peak and then returns to its starting level. For a person with untreated Type 1 diabetes it rises higher and stays high. What does the graph show about the person with Type 1 diabetes?

options.text: not enough insulin is produced to lower glucose
options.rationale: The concentration stays high because the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, so glucose is not moved from the blood into the cells and the level is not brought back down.

options.text: their body cells have stopped responding to insulin
options.rationale: A student who confuses the two types of diabetes picks this. It is wrong because cells that no longer respond to insulin describe Type 2 diabetes; in Type 1 the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin.

options.text: their insulin cannot change glucose to glycogen
options.rationale: A student who thinks insulin converts glucose in the blood picks this. It is wrong because insulin moves glucose into cells, where excess glucose is converted to glycogen in liver and muscle cells.

options.text: their insulin is produced when glucose is low
options.rationale: A student who reverses the trigger for insulin release picks this. It is wrong because insulin is produced when the blood glucose concentration is too high, which is the situation shown on the graph.

mcqs.stem: Several hours after a meal, the blood glucose concentration of a person falls below the normal level. Which change restores it?

options.text: insulin is released and stored glycogen changes to glucose
options.rationale: A student who treats insulin and glucagon as interchangeable picks this. It is wrong because insulin is produced when the concentration is too high; glucagon is the hormone that releases glucose from glycogen.

options.text: glucagon is released and glucose changes to glycogen
options.rationale: A student who confuses glucagon with glycogen picks this. It is wrong because storing glucose as glycogen would lower the concentration further, while glucagon converts glycogen into glucose.

options.text: glucagon is released and glycogen changes to glucose
options.rationale: If the blood glucose concentration is too low, the pancreas produces glucagon, which causes glycogen to be converted into glucose and released into the blood.

options.text: insulin is released and glucose changes to glycogen
options.rationale: A student who thinks insulin acts when glucose is too low picks this. It is wrong because this response lowers the blood glucose concentration, and insulin is produced when it is too high.

mcqs.stem: The body fluids around a person's cells become too dilute. What is the effect on the cells?

options.text: they gain water by osmosis and work as normal
options.rationale: A student who believes osmotic change does not matter picks this. It is wrong because if body cells gain too much water by osmosis they do not function efficiently.

options.text: they gain water by osmosis and work less well
options.rationale: Water moves into the cells by osmosis from the more dilute body fluids, and if body cells gain too much water by osmosis they do not function efficiently.

options.text: they lose water by osmosis and stop working well
options.rationale: A student who reverses the direction of osmosis picks this. It is wrong because water moves into cells when the fluid around them is too dilute, so the cells gain water.

options.text: they lose water by osmosis and work as normal
options.rationale: A student who reverses the direction of osmosis and also expects no effect picks this. It is wrong because the cells gain water, and cells that gain too much water do not function efficiently.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the loss of water and other substances from the body is correct?

options.text: water lost in sweat is controlled by hormones
options.rationale: A student who assumes all water loss is regulated picks this. It is wrong because there is no control over water, ion or urea loss by the lungs or skin.

options.text: sweat contains water but no ions or urea
options.rationale: A student who thinks of sweat only as water for cooling picks this. It is wrong because water, ions and urea are lost from the skin in sweat.

options.text: water lost from the lungs is not controlled
options.rationale: Water leaves the body via the lungs during exhalation, and there is no control over water, ion or urea loss by the lungs or skin.

options.text: water lost from the skin is closely controlled
options.rationale: A student who links controlled sweating in temperature regulation to water balance picks this. It is wrong because there is no control over water, ion or urea loss by the skin.

mcqs.stem: How do the kidneys produce urine and help to maintain the water balance of the body?

options.text: only waste substances are filtered out of the blood
options.rationale: A student who pictures filtration as a one-step sieve picks this. It is wrong because useful substances are filtered out too, and are then taken back by selective reabsorption.

options.text: glucose and all useful ions are lost in the urine
options.rationale: A student who believes everything dissolved is removed from the blood picks this. It is wrong because useful substances such as glucose, some ions and water are selectively reabsorbed.

options.text: urea is reabsorbed and glucose is lost in the urine
options.rationale: A student who is unsure which substances are kept picks this. It is wrong because glucose is a useful substance that is reabsorbed, while excess urea is removed in the urine.

options.text: the blood is filtered and useful substances reabsorbed
options.rationale: The kidneys produce urine by filtration of the blood and selective reabsorption of useful substances such as glucose, some ions and water, and excess water, ions and urea are removed in the urine.

mcqs.stem: A table gives the concentration of two substances in the blood entering a kidney and in the urine leaving it, in grams per dm3. Glucose: 1.0 in the blood and 0.0 in the urine. Urea: 0.3 in the blood and 20.0 in the urine. What do these figures show?

options.text: glucose is not filtered, so none reaches the urine
options.rationale: A student who believes useful substances never leave the blood picks this. It is wrong because glucose is filtered out of the blood and then returned by selective reabsorption.

options.text: glucose is reabsorbed, so it is absent from urine
options.rationale: The blood is filtered and glucose is a useful substance that is selectively reabsorbed, so its concentration in the urine falls to zero while urea becomes concentrated.

options.text: glucose is removed with the urea and lost from blood
options.rationale: A student who believes useful substances are taken out along with waste picks this. It is wrong because glucose is reabsorbed into the blood, which is why none of it appears in the urine.

options.text: urea and glucose are both reabsorbed by the kidney
options.rationale: A student who is unsure which substances are kept picks this. It is wrong because the urea figures show it is concentrated in the urine, not returned to the blood.

mcqs.stem: On a hot day a person sweats a great deal and drinks very little, so the blood becomes too concentrated. What is the effect of ADH on the kidney tubules?

options.text: they become less permeable, so water is reabsorbed
options.rationale: A student who knows water must be saved but reverses the effect on the tubules picks this. It is wrong because ADH makes the kidney tubules more permeable, which is how more water is reabsorbed.

options.text: they become more permeable, so more urine is produced
options.rationale: A student who thinks ADH removes water picks this. It is wrong because water is reabsorbed back into the blood when the blood is too concentrated, so less urine is produced.

options.text: they become more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed
options.rationale: ADH is released by the pituitary gland when the blood is too concentrated and acts on the kidney tubules, making them more permeable so that more water is reabsorbed back into the blood.

options.text: they become less permeable, so more sweat is produced
options.rationale: A student who believes water loss in sweat is controlled picks this. It is wrong because there is no control over water loss by the skin, and ADH acts on the kidney tubules.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes a basic principle of kidney dialysis?

options.text: glucose passes from the blood into the dialysis fluid
options.rationale: A student who believes dialysis strips everything from the blood picks this. It is wrong because the dialysis fluid contains the same concentration of glucose as normal blood, so glucose is not lost.

options.text: urea passes from the blood into the dialysis fluid
options.rationale: Dialysis treats kidney failure by allowing urea to pass out of the blood into a dialysis fluid that contains no urea, while useful substances are not lost.

options.text: useful ions pass from the blood into the fluid
options.rationale: A student who thinks the blood is washed clean of everything picks this. It is wrong because the dialysis fluid contains the useful ions at their normal blood concentration, so they stay in the blood.

options.text: water and ions pass from the blood into the fluid
options.rationale: A student who believes all dissolved substances are removed picks this. It is wrong because the fluid is made so that useful substances are kept; it is the excess urea that is removed.

mcqs.stem: What is the role of follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) in the menstrual cycle?

options.text: it causes a mature egg to be released
options.rationale: A student who swaps the roles of the two hormones picks this. It is wrong because luteinising hormone (LH) stimulates the release of the egg.

options.text: it keeps the lining of the uterus in place
options.rationale: A student who exchanges the roles of the two pairs of hormones picks this. It is wrong because oestrogen and progesterone are involved in maintaining the uterus lining.

options.text: it causes an egg to mature in the ovary
options.rationale: Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) causes maturation of an egg in the ovary.

options.text: it is released from the ovary at puberty
options.rationale: A student who is unsure which gland makes each hormone picks this. It is wrong because oestrogen is the hormone produced in the ovary; FSH acts on the ovary to mature an egg.

mcqs.stem: Which interaction between hormones helps to control the menstrual cycle?

options.text: LH inhibits FSH and causes an egg to mature
options.rationale: A student who swaps the roles of FSH and LH picks this. It is wrong because FSH causes maturation of an egg in the ovary and LH stimulates its release.

options.text: FSH inhibits oestrogen and maintains the lining
options.rationale: A student who exchanges the roles of the two pairs of hormones picks this. It is wrong because FSH causes an egg to mature, while oestrogen and progesterone maintain the uterus lining.

options.text: progesterone stimulates FSH and LH release
options.rationale: A student who gives progesterone the job of controlling the egg picks this. It is wrong because progesterone is involved in maintaining the uterus lining and inhibits FSH and LH.

options.text: oestrogen inhibits FSH and stimulates LH release
options.rationale: Oestrogen produced in the ovary inhibits the production of FSH and stimulates the release of LH, which then stimulates the release of the egg.

mcqs.stem: A graph of hormone levels during the menstrual cycle shows the level of LH rising to a sharp peak on day 14. What is happening on day 14?

options.text: an egg is starting to mature in the ovary
options.rationale: A student who swaps the roles of FSH and LH picks this. It is wrong because maturation of the egg is caused by FSH, whose level rises earlier in the cycle.

options.text: an egg is being released from the ovary
options.rationale: Luteinising hormone (LH) stimulates the release of the egg, so a sharp peak in LH on day 14 indicates ovulation.

options.text: the lining of the uterus is being maintained
options.rationale: A student who gives LH the job of the other pair of hormones picks this. It is wrong because the uterus lining is maintained by oestrogen and progesterone, not by the LH peak.

options.text: the lining of the uterus is breaking down
options.rationale: A student who links LH to the uterus rather than the ovary picks this. It is wrong because LH acts on the ovary to stimulate the release of the egg.

mcqs.stem: A woman wants a method of contraception that does not use hormones. Which method and reason are correct?

options.text: a condom, which releases a hormone slowly
options.rationale: A student who thinks all contraceptives involve hormones picks this. It is wrong because a condom is a barrier method that prevents the sperm reaching an egg and contains no hormone.

options.text: a diaphragm, which stops sperm reaching eggs
options.rationale: Barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms prevent the sperm reaching an egg, so they control fertility without using hormones.

options.text: the pill, which kills sperm before they arrive
options.rationale: A student who believes the pill acts on sperm picks this. It is wrong because oral contraceptives contain hormones to inhibit FSH production so that no eggs mature.

options.text: an implant, which stops sperm reaching an egg
options.rationale: A student who confuses the mechanisms of the different methods picks this. It is wrong because an implant releases slow release progesterone to inhibit the maturation and release of eggs.

mcqs.stem: How do oral contraceptives that contain hormones prevent pregnancy?

options.text: they inhibit FSH production so no eggs mature
options.rationale: Oral contraceptives contain hormones to inhibit FSH production so that no eggs mature.

options.text: they kill or disable sperm before fertilisation
options.rationale: A student who gives every contraceptive the same mechanism picks this. It is wrong because killing or disabling sperm is the action of spermicidal agents.

options.text: they stop an embryo implanting in the uterus
options.rationale: A student who attaches the wrong mechanism to the method picks this. It is wrong because preventing the implantation of an embryo is the action of an intrauterine device.

options.text: they form a barrier that stops sperm reaching eggs
options.rationale: A student who mixes up hormonal and barrier methods picks this. It is wrong because condoms and diaphragms are the barrier methods; the pill inhibits FSH production.

mcqs.stem: A woman does not release eggs because her level of FSH is too low. Which treatment could allow her to become pregnant in the normal way?

options.text: a fertility drug that contains FSH and LH
options.rationale: Giving FSH and LH in a 'fertility drug' to a woman stimulates the maturation and release of eggs, and she may then become pregnant in the normal way.

options.text: a fertility drug that contains progesterone
options.rationale: A student who gives progesterone the job of maturing eggs picks this. It is wrong because progesterone is involved in maintaining the uterus lining; the fertility drug contains FSH and LH.

options.text: IVF, in which eggs are fertilised in her body
options.rationale: A student who thinks IVF fertilisation happens inside the mother picks this. It is wrong because in IVF the eggs are collected and fertilised in the laboratory, not in the normal way.

options.text: a fertility drug that contains only LH
options.rationale: A student who thinks LH matures the eggs picks this. It is wrong because FSH causes maturation of an egg, so both FSH and LH are given in the fertility drug.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about IVF treatment is correct?

options.text: eggs are fertilised by sperm in the laboratory
options.rationale: In IVF the eggs are collected from the mother and fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory; the embryos are inserted into the uterus as tiny balls of cells.

options.text: eggs are fertilised by the sperm inside the mother
options.rationale: A student who treats IVF as an ordinary pregnancy helped by hormones picks this. It is wrong because the eggs are collected from the mother and fertilised in the laboratory.

options.text: most IVF treatments result in a successful birth
options.rationale: A student who has only heard about successful IVF births picks this. It is wrong because the success rates of fertility treatment are not high.

options.text: multiple births from IVF carry very little risk
options.rationale: A student who sees multiple births as a happy outcome picks this. It is wrong because IVF can lead to multiple births which are a risk to both the babies and the mother.

mcqs.stem: A student is suddenly frightened by a loud noise. Which gland releases adrenaline, and what effect does it have?

options.text: the adrenal gland; it raises the heart rate
options.rationale: Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress; it increases the heart rate and boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles.

options.text: the pituitary gland; it raises the heart rate
options.rationale: A student who makes the master gland the source of the emergency hormone picks this. It is wrong because adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands.

options.text: the thyroid gland; it reduces the heart rate
options.rationale: A student who thinks the thyroid gland slows the body down picks this. It is wrong because thyroxine from the thyroid stimulates the basal metabolic rate, and adrenaline comes from the adrenal glands.

options.text: the pituitary gland; it lowers the heart rate
options.rationale: A student who names the wrong gland and reverses the effect picks this. It is wrong because the adrenal glands produce adrenaline, which increases the heart rate for 'flight or fight'.

mcqs.stem: The concentration of thyroxine in the blood of a person rises above the normal level. What happens next?

options.text: more thyroxine is released and the level rises
options.rationale: A student who thinks feedback adds to a change picks this. It is wrong because thyroxine levels are controlled by negative feedback, which returns the level to normal.

options.text: the metabolic rate falls and the level stays high
options.rationale: A student who believes thyroxine lowers the metabolic rate picks this. It is wrong because thyroxine stimulates the basal metabolic rate, and its own level is returned to normal.

options.text: the metabolic rate falls and more thyroxine forms
options.rationale: A student who reverses the effect of thyroxine picks this. It is wrong because thyroxine stimulates the basal metabolic rate, and a level above normal inhibits further release.

options.text: thyroxine release is inhibited and the level falls
options.rationale: Thyroxine levels are controlled by negative feedback, so a level above normal inhibits the release of thyroxine until the level returns to normal.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the main reproductive hormones is correct?

options.text: oestrogen is produced by the pituitary gland
options.rationale: A student who makes the master gland the source of every hormone picks this. It is wrong because oestrogen is the main female reproductive hormone produced in the ovary.

options.text: testosterone is produced by the testes
options.rationale: Testosterone is the main male reproductive hormone produced by the testes, and it stimulates sperm production.

options.text: oestrogen is produced by the thyroid gland
options.rationale: A student who has not linked each gland to its hormone picks this. It is wrong because the thyroid gland produces thyroxine, while oestrogen is produced in the ovary.

options.text: testosterone is produced by the pituitary
options.rationale: A student who believes the pituitary gland makes the reproductive hormones picks this. It is wrong because testosterone is produced by the testes.
